core_insights.generalization: For any high-frequency, low-variance task with a stable instruction set, the build-vs-prompt decision is fundamentally an amortization calculation: (calls per period x cached-input cost) vs (training run cost + eval/refresh overhead).
core_insights.insight: There is a structural trade-off between expressing organizational knowledge in the context window (re-explained/cached on every call) and baking it into model weights via a training run. core_insights.why_it_matters: Agent workloads that re-supply the same large context on every call carry a per-invocation cost and latency floor. Moving repeatable workflows into weights converts a recurring token cost into a one-time training cost, which changes how you budget and architect an agent stack.

core_insights.why_it_matters: This places routing responsibility in the harness layer rather than in application code or a static config, which means routing policy becomes something you evaluate, version, and monitor like any other model — and it is the mechanism that makes a mixed frontier/custom model portfolio economically viable.

core_insights.why_it_matters: This reframes the eval suite as the primary engineering interface for a model, and turns retraining into a scheduled CI-like step rather than a one-off project. document.description: One-paragraph summary of Your Company Should Train Its Own AI Models - Will Brown, Prime Intellect

key_claims.claim: Cached input in agent workflows is a cost bottleneck that training into weights can relieve.
key_claims.evidence: Addresses the bottleneck and cost of cached inputs in agent workflows.
key_claims.verification_question: What is the actual per-call cost and latency contribution of cached input in representative agent workloads, and at what call volume does a training run amortize?

key_claims.claim: Model capability gains across generations stem partly from training on high-value repeatable workflows, not only from prompt improvements.
key_claims.evidence: Models get better with new generations not just because prompts improve, but because they are trained more on high-value repeatable workflows.
key_claims.verification_question: Can capability gains be decomposed between prompt/context changes and additional training on repeatable workflows?

key_claims.claim: Decision models in an agent harness can route tasks between frontier and custom models by cost, latency, and capability.
key_claims.evidence: Decision models in agent harnesses can route tasks between expensive frontier models and cheaper custom-trained models based on cost, latency, and capability.
key_claims.verification_question: What quality delta results from routing compared to always using the frontier model, and how often does the router misclassify task difficulty?

key_claims.claim: Evals can function as test cases for models, mirroring the software development lifecycle.
key_claims.evidence: Evals can act as test cases for models, mirroring software development lifecycles.
key_claims.verification_question: Which properties of software test suites (determinism, pass/fail thresholds, coverage) transfer to non-deterministic model evals, and which break down?

key_claims.claim: Organizational preferences and friction exist as patterns in data rather than as written rules.
key_claims.evidence: Scripts and procedures are written down as rules, but preferences and friction live as patterns in data.

key_claims.claim: Agents are effective at combing unstructured textual organizational data to surface patterns and friction.
key_claims.evidence: Agents are great at combing through unstructured textual data to surface patterns, preferences, and friction.
key_claims.verification_question: How precisely can agent-driven extraction recover institutional decision patterns from raw communications, and what is the human review burden?

key_claims.claim: A specialized knowledge-work model was trained for $300k by a team of five, making custom training a practical alternative to hiring.
key_claims.evidence: Paper Instruments training a model for $300k with a team of five people.
key_claims.verification_question: Does the $300k include data preparation, eval construction, and ongoing maintenance, and what is the measured performance versus frontier baselines?

key_claims.claim: Nightly feedback loops allow continuous retraining of checkpoints from production traces and human feedback.
key_claims.evidence: Nightly feedback loops allow organizations to continuously retrain checkpoints using production traces and human feedback.
key_claims.verification_question: Does nightly retraining produce measurable improvement over a static checkpoint once eval-gating and feedback noise are accounted for?

open_questions.question: What operational threshold makes a workflow a candidate for training rather than context? Can the 'high-value repeatable workflow' criterion be operationalized as a measurable signal (call volume, context size, output variance)?
open_questions.research_direction: Instrument agent traces per task family (calls/period, context tokens, output stability) and compare modeled per-call context cost against fully-loaded training cost to derive an empirical break-even curve.
open_questions.why_unresolved: The summary asserts the trade-off exists and references a graph, but gives no quantitative criteria, break-even point, or measurement method.

open_questions.question: How is the routing decision model itself evaluated and kept calibrated as frontier model pricing, latency, and capability change?
open_questions.research_direction: Build a routing eval that replays labeled traces through both routes and measures quality delta against cost delta; treat routing as a policy that can itself be fine-tuned.
open_questions.why_unresolved: The summary describes routing by cost, latency, and capability but provides no mechanism for scoring routing decisions or detecting misroutes.

open_questions.question: What guards a nightly retraining loop against regression or collapse when trained on self-generated production traces and noisy human feedback?
open_questions.research_direction: Prototype a gated loop with fixed holdout eval suites, shadow-mode checkpoints, and automatic rollback; measure regression rate over successive nightly iterations.
open_questions.why_unresolved: The summary describes checkpoint scoring and nightly training but does not state holdout discipline, promotion gates, or how human feedback is filtered.

open_questions.question: How can patterns be extracted from unstructured communications data at organizational scale without leaking sensitive information into weights?
open_questions.research_direction: Design a provenance-tagged extraction pipeline where each training sample is traceable to source and access scope, and test whether scrubbing is verifiable post-training.
open_questions.why_unresolved: The summary recommends agents mine emails, meetings, and tacit knowledge but says nothing about data governance, access boundaries, or unlearning.

open_questions.question: Does a fine-tuned custom model retain general reasoning ability, or does specialization trade broad capability for domain accuracy in a way that routing must compensate for?
open_questions.research_direction: Evaluate specialized checkpoints on both in-domain evals and a held-out general capability suite to quantify the specialization tax.
open_questions.why_unresolved: The summary frames custom models as cheaper substitutes for frontier models on routine work but provides no measurement of capability degradation outside the target domain.

project_ideas.based_on: amortization calculation: (calls per period x cached-input cost) vs (training run cost + eval/refresh overhead)
project_ideas.hypothesis: Given a task family's call volume, context size, and output variance, a model built from trace telemetry can predict the context-vs-training cost crossover within one order of magnitude, and the predicted crossover matches the empirically observed one after a training run.
project_ideas.measurement: Absolute error between predicted and observed crossover volume; whether the ranking of task families by training-eligibility matches the ranking produced by post-hoc real costs.
project_ideas.name: Amortization Instrument
project_ideas.poc: Instrument agent traces to log calls/period, context tokens, and output stability per task family; compute per-call context cost against a fully-loaded training cost estimate; then run one real training job on the top-ranked task family and compare predicted versus actual total spend at 1x, 10x, and 100x projected volume.

project_ideas.based_on: a decision model that misjudges capability sends hard tasks to the cheap model
project_ideas.hypothesis: A replay-based routing eval that runs labeled traces through both the frontier and the custom model can detect capability misclassifications before they reach production, and routers tuned against this signal reduce quality delta on hard tasks without losing most of the cost savings.
project_ideas.measurement: Misroute rate on labeled hard tasks; quality delta versus always-frontier baseline; fraction of cost savings retained after gating.
project_ideas.name: Misroute Gate
project_ideas.poc: Build a replay harness over captured production traces with per-trace labels for task difficulty and reference outputs; score both routes; construct a quality-delta-vs-cost-delta frontier; then deploy a routing threshold as a promotion gate that blocks rollout when misroute rate on labeled hard tasks exceeds a set bound.

project_ideas.based_on: Prototype a gated loop with fixed holdout eval suites, shadow-mode checkpoints, and automatic rollback
project_ideas.hypothesis: A nightly retrain loop with fixed holdout eval suites, shadow-mode checkpoints, and automatic rollback produces measurable improvement over a static checkpoint across successive iterations, while an ungated nightly loop of the same design drifts or regresses within a small number of cycles.
project_ideas.measurement: Per-iteration score deltas on holdout suites; regression rate per cycle; rollback frequency; divergence between gated and ungated curves over 10+ cycles.
project_ideas.name: Shadow Retrain Loop
project_ideas.poc: Run two identical nightly retraining pipelines on the same production traces and human feedback stream, one with the promotion gate and one without; log in-domain and holdout scores per iteration and record every automatic rollback.

project_ideas.based_on: Does a fine-tuned custom model retain general reasoning ability
project_ideas.hypothesis: A custom checkpoint trained on a narrow knowledge-work domain loses a measurable and quantifiable amount of capability on a held-out general suite, and that measured loss is a better input to the router's difficulty estimate than a blanket capability assumption.
project_ideas.measurement: In-domain accuracy gain versus out-of-domain capability drop; end-to-end task success and cost per task with the measured versus assumed routing policy.
project_ideas.name: Specialization Tax Bench
project_ideas.poc: Train or obtain one narrow domain checkpoint; evaluate it on both in-domain tasks and a held-out general capability suite alongside the frontier baseline; then feed the measured per-category deltas into a routing policy and compare end-to-end quality and cost against a routing policy that assumes equal capability.

summary.html:
Overview

  • Speaker: Will Brown
  • Channel: AI Engineer
  • Main topic: Self-improving organizations and training custom AI models at enterprise scale
  • Purpose: To outline how organizations can transition from using off-the-shelf frontier models to training custom, self-improving models that compound institutional knowledge and advantages. Will Brown, Head of Applied Research at Prime Intellect, discusses the evolution of AI adoption from chatbots to reasoning agents, innovators, and ultimately self-improving organizations. He argues that organizations must move beyond cached input and prompt engineering to train custom knowledge work models using their internal data, workflows, and feedback loops, treating models much like codebases with version control, evals, and continuous learning.

Topic Map

From Chatbots to Organizations

  • Explanation: Tracing the progression of AI capabilities from early chatbots and reasoners to agents, innovators, and enterprise-wide organizational integration.
  • Key claims:
    • AI adoption has moved faster than expected through reasoners, agents, and innovators.
    • The next frontier is AI-native organizations with deep agent integration throughout their lifecycle.
  • Examples:
    • OpenAI's levels of AI capability framework.
  • Terminology:
    • chatbots
    • reasoners
    • agents
    • innovators
    • organizations
  • Why it matters: Helps organizations understand the trajectory of AI maturity and where enterprise value is heading.

What Organizations Know vs. What Models Learn

  • Explanation: Comparing implicit, institutional knowledge stored in people's heads and unstructured communications versus explicit knowledge captured in codebases and procedures.
  • Key claims:
    • Much of a company's valuable institutional knowledge lives implicitly in people's heads and between the lines of emails and meetings.
    • Agents are great at combing through unstructured textual data to surface patterns, preferences, and friction.
  • Examples:
    • Org charts on paper versus real organizational decision-making dynamics.
  • Terminology:
    • implicit knowledge
    • explicit knowledge
    • org chart
    • friction
  • Why it matters: Highlights the knowledge gap between human employees and AI models that custom training aims to bridge.

Rules and Patterns: Code vs. Data

  • Explanation: Contrasting rules that live in code (scripts, skills, procedures) against patterns that live in data (preferences, friction, heuristics, trends).
  • Key claims:
    • Scripts and procedures are written down as rules, but preferences and friction live as patterns in data.
    • Employees implicitly learn institutional patterns that standard models never get a chance to learn.
  • Examples:
    • Coding vs data spectrum.
  • Terminology:
    • rules
    • patterns
    • heuristics
    • friction
  • Why it matters: Explains why prompt engineering and context windows alone are insufficient for capturing deep organizational expertise.

Context or Weights

  • Explanation: Evaluating when to rely on context windows versus baking knowledge into model weights through training.
  • Key claims:
    • Models get better with new generations not just because prompts improve, but because they are trained more on high-value repeatable workflows.
    • Training allows compounding of institutional knowledge into model weights.
  • Examples:
    • Training run vs explained-on-every-call trade-off graph.
  • Terminology:
    • context window
    • weights
    • training run
    • cached input
  • Why it matters: Addresses the bottleneck and cost of cached inputs in agent workflows.

Evals as Test Cases and Decisions & Routing

  • Explanation: Treating AI models like codebases by implementing evaluation test cases, agent traces, and cost-optimized model routing.
  • Key claims:
    • Evals can act as test cases for models, mirroring software development lifecycles.
    • Decision models in agent harnesses can route tasks between expensive frontier models and cheaper custom-trained models based on cost, latency, and capability.
  • Examples:
    • Claims triage nightly model eval grid.
    • Decision cards UI interface.
  • Terminology:
    • evals
    • traces
    • harness
    • decision model
    • routing
  • Why it matters: Provides a practical methodology for managing, evaluating, and cost-optimizing model stacks.

Custom Knowledge Work Models & Nightly Loops

  • Explanation: Real-world examples of custom knowledge work models trained on domain data and deployed in continuous nightly improvement loops.
  • Key claims:
    • Training custom domain models (e.g., for spreadsheets and slides) is becoming a practical alternative to hiring additional software engineers.
    • Nightly feedback loops allow organizations to continuously retrain checkpoints using production traces and human feedback.
  • Examples:
    • Paper Instruments training a model for $300k with a team of five people.
    • Nightly checkpoint scoring and training prototype loop.
  • Terminology:
    • knowledge work models
    • nightly loop
    • checkpoint
    • continuous learning
  • Why it matters: Demonstrates the economic and operational feasibility of enterprise model training.

Key Points

Organizations possess vast implicit knowledge that is hard to capture in code

  • Explanation: Company procedures, decisions, and judgment norms live across employee interactions, meeting notes, and unwritten practices.
  • Evidence: Comparison between written procedures/systems and human-held institutional knowledge.
  • Practical implication: AI agents must be leveraged to sift through unstructured organizational data to surface patterns and tacit knowledge.

Treating models like codebases unlocks continuous improvement

  • Explanation: Just as software engineering uses unit tests, CI/CD, and version control, AI models need test cases (evals), traces, and systematic lifecycles.
  • Evidence: Analogy between software development lifecycles and model evaluation workflows.
  • Practical implication: Organizing model training around robust evals and traces enables compounding institutional advantage.

Custom training is becoming economically viable for enterprises

  • Explanation: Organizations can invest in training custom models on proprietary domain workflows rather than repeatedly paying for expensive cached inputs on frontier models.
  • Evidence: Example of Paper Instruments spending $300k with a small team to train a specialized model for spreadsheets and slides.
  • Practical implication: Enterprises can treat model training as an internal HR/engineering investment to compound institutional knowledge.

Frameworks, Models & Processes

The Prime Intellect Stack

  • How it works: A modular infrastructure stack combining platform capabilities (training, inference, observability, evaluations, sandboxes, research partnerships) with open-source tools (verifiers, prime-r1, Prime Agent, Intellect series).
  • Components:
    • Training
    • Inference
    • Observability
    • Evaluations
    • Sandboxes
    • Verifiers
    • Prime Agent
  • When to use: When building, training, and deploying open-source models and agent workflows at scale.

The Adoption Path

  • How it works: A progressive maturity model for organizations adopting AI, moving from single-person workflow discovery to enterprise-wide continual training.
  • Components:
    • Workflow discovery
    • Skills
    • Evals
    • Routing
    • Continual training
  • When to use: When planning an enterprise roadmap for AI adoption and agent integration.

Examples & Case Studies

Paper Instruments trained a custom model tailored for knowledge work like spreadsheets and slides.

  • Illustrates: The economic feasibility of custom knowledge work models for organizations.
  • Lesson: Investing in custom domain model training can yield high organizational ROI compared to relying solely on general frontier models.

Actionable Takeaways

  • Immediate:
    • Implement tracing and evaluation test cases for your agent workflows.
    • Identify high-value repeatable workflows suitable for model routing and training.
  • Strategic:
    • Shift from prompt engineering and cached context to training custom knowledge work models.
    • Establish nightly continuous learning loops that retrain model checkpoints on organizational data and feedback.
  • Questions to investigate:
    • How can our organization effectively turn production traces into robust evaluation environments?
    • What is the cost-benefit threshold for training custom models versus using frontier inference APIs?

Claims Worth Verifying

  • Custom domain models for spreadsheets and slides can be trained for around $300k with a small team. (empirical)

Notable Quotes

"What are the different stages of AI progress on the road to AGI? And I think we've moved along this faster than we thought we would." "Organizations have lots of knowledge and like the longer an organization's been around and the kind of more established it is, the more implicit knowledge there is that kind of doesn't ever get written down." "The models get better not because the prompt is better, but because they train them more. Like training is useful, training works, training is why we see the progress we do."

Compressed Summary

  • AI adoption is progressing from chatbots and reasoners to autonomous organizations.
  • Prompt engineering and cached inputs create bottlenecks and high costs in agent workflows.
  • Enterprises should treat AI models like codebases with test cases, evals, and traces.
  • Custom knowledge work models allow companies to bake implicit institutional knowledge into model weights.
  • Nightly loops enable automated continuous learning and checkpoint improvement.
  • Keywords: agents, evals, training, routing, continual-learning
  • Core insight: Organizations must transition from relying on prompt engineering and cached context to training custom models on their own data and workflows, establishing continuous feedback loops to compound institutional knowledge into model weights.

- **Purpose**: To outline how organizations can transition from using off-the-shelf frontier models to training custom, self-improving models that compound institutional knowledge and advantages.
Will Brown, Head of Applied Research at Prime Intellect, discusses the evolution of AI adoption from chatbots to reasoning agents, innovators, and ultimately self-improving organizations. He argues that organizations must move beyond cached input and prompt engineering to train custom knowledge work models using their internal data, workflows, and feedback loops, treating models much like codebases with version control, evals, and continuous learning.
## Topic Map
### From Chatbots to Organizations
- **Explanation**: Tracing the progression of AI capabilities from early chatbots and reasoners to agents, innovators, and enterprise-wide organizational integration.
- **Key claims**:
  - AI adoption has moved faster than expected through reasoners, agents, and innovators.
  - The next frontier is AI-native organizations with deep agent integration throughout their lifecycle.
- **Examples**:
  - OpenAI's levels of AI capability framework.
- **Terminology**:
  - chatbots
  - reasoners
  - agents
  - innovators
  - organizations
- **Why it matters**: Helps organizations understand the trajectory of AI maturity and where enterprise value is heading.
### What Organizations Know vs. What Models Learn
- **Explanation**: Comparing implicit, institutional knowledge stored in people's heads and unstructured communications versus explicit knowledge captured in codebases and procedures.
- **Key claims**:
  - Much of a company's valuable institutional knowledge lives implicitly in people's heads and between the lines of emails and meetings.
  - Agents are great at combing through unstructured textual data to surface patterns, preferences, and friction.
- **Examples**:
  - Org charts on paper versus real organizational decision-making dynamics.
- **Terminology**:
  - implicit knowledge
  - explicit knowledge
  - org chart
  - friction
- **Why it matters**: Highlights the knowledge gap between human employees and AI models that custom training aims to bridge.
### Rules and Patterns: Code vs. Data
- **Explanation**: Contrasting rules that live in code (scripts, skills, procedures) against patterns that live in data (preferences, friction, heuristics, trends).
- **Key claims**:
  - Scripts and procedures are written down as rules, but preferences and friction live as patterns in data.
  - Employees implicitly learn institutional patterns that standard models never get a chance to learn.
- **Examples**:
  - Coding vs data spectrum.
- **Terminology**:
  - rules
  - patterns
  - heuristics
  - friction
- **Why it matters**: Explains why prompt engineering and context windows alone are insufficient for capturing deep organizational expertise.
### Context or Weights
- **Explanation**: Evaluating when to rely on context windows versus baking knowledge into model weights through training.
- **Key claims**:
  - Models get better with new generations not just because prompts improve, but because they are trained more on high-value repeatable workflows.
  - Training allows compounding of institutional knowledge into model weights.
- **Examples**:
  - Training run vs explained-on-every-call trade-off graph.
- **Terminology**:
  - context window
  - weights
  - training run
  - cached input
- **Why it matters**: Addresses the bottleneck and cost of cached inputs in agent workflows.
### Evals as Test Cases and Decisions & Routing
- **Explanation**: Treating AI models like codebases by implementing evaluation test cases, agent traces, and cost-optimized model routing.
- **Key claims**:
  - Evals can act as test cases for models, mirroring software development lifecycles.
  - Decision models in agent harnesses can route tasks between expensive frontier models and cheaper custom-trained models based on cost, latency, and capability.
- **Examples**:
  - Claims triage nightly model eval grid.
  - Decision cards UI interface.
- **Terminology**:
  - evals
  - traces
  - harness
  - decision model
  - routing
- **Why it matters**: Provides a practical methodology for managing, evaluating, and cost-optimizing model stacks.
### Custom Knowledge Work Models & Nightly Loops
- **Explanation**: Real-world examples of custom knowledge work models trained on domain data and deployed in continuous nightly improvement loops.
- **Key claims**:
  - Training custom domain models (e.g., for spreadsheets and slides) is becoming a practical alternative to hiring additional software engineers.
  - Nightly feedback loops allow organizations to continuously retrain checkpoints using production traces and human feedback.
- **Examples**:
  - Paper Instruments training a model for $300k with a team of five people.
  - Nightly checkpoint scoring and training prototype loop.
- **Terminology**:
  - knowledge work models
  - nightly loop
  - checkpoint
  - continuous learning
- **Why it matters**: Demonstrates the economic and operational feasibility of enterprise model training.
## Key Points
### Organizations possess vast implicit knowledge that is hard to capture in code
- **Explanation**: Company procedures, decisions, and judgment norms live across employee interactions, meeting notes, and unwritten practices.
- **Evidence**: Comparison between written procedures/systems and human-held institutional knowledge.
- **Practical implication**: AI agents must be leveraged to sift through unstructured organizational data to surface patterns and tacit knowledge.
### Treating models like codebases unlocks continuous improvement
- **Explanation**: Just as software engineering uses unit tests, CI/CD, and version control, AI models need test cases (evals), traces, and systematic lifecycles.
- **Evidence**: Analogy between software development lifecycles and model evaluation workflows.
- **Practical implication**: Organizing model training around robust evals and traces enables compounding institutional advantage.
### Custom training is becoming economically viable for enterprises
- **Explanation**: Organizations can invest in training custom models on proprietary domain workflows rather than repeatedly paying for expensive cached inputs on frontier models.
- **Evidence**: Example of Paper Instruments spending $300k with a small team to train a specialized model for spreadsheets and slides.
- **Practical implication**: Enterprises can treat model training as an internal HR/engineering investment to compound institutional knowledge.
## Frameworks, Models & Processes
### The Prime Intellect Stack
- **How it works**: A modular infrastructure stack combining platform capabilities (training, inference, observability, evaluations, sandboxes, research partnerships) with open-source tools (verifiers, prime-r1, Prime Agent, Intellect series).
- **Components**:
  - Training
  - Inference
  - Observability
  - Evaluations
  - Sandboxes
  - Verifiers
  - Prime Agent
- **When to use**: When building, training, and deploying open-source models and agent workflows at scale.
### The Adoption Path
- **How it works**: A progressive maturity model for organizations adopting AI, moving from single-person workflow discovery to enterprise-wide continual training.
- **Components**:
  - Workflow discovery
  - Skills
  - Evals
  - Routing
  - Continual training
- **When to use**: When planning an enterprise roadmap for AI adoption and agent integration.
## Examples & Case Studies
### Paper Instruments trained a custom model tailored for knowledge work like spreadsheets and slides.
- **Illustrates**: The economic feasibility of custom knowledge work models for organizations.
- **Lesson**: Investing in custom domain model training can yield high organizational ROI compared to relying solely on general frontier models.
## Actionable Takeaways
- **Immediate**:
  - Implement tracing and evaluation test cases for your agent workflows.
  - Identify high-value repeatable workflows suitable for model routing and training.
- **Strategic**:
  - Shift from prompt engineering and cached context to training custom knowledge work models.
  - Establish nightly continuous learning loops that retrain model checkpoints on organizational data and feedback.
- **Questions to investigate**:
  - How can our organization effectively turn production traces into robust evaluation environments?
  - What is the cost-benefit threshold for training custom models versus using frontier inference APIs?
## Claims Worth Verifying
- Custom domain models for spreadsheets and slides can be trained for around $300k with a small team. (empirical)
## Notable Quotes
> "What are the different stages of AI progress on the road to AGI? And I think we've moved along this faster than we thought we would."
> "Organizations have lots of knowledge and like the longer an organization's been around and the kind of more established it is, the more implicit knowledge there is that kind of doesn't ever get written down."
> "The models get better not because the prompt is better, but because they train them more. Like training is useful, training works, training is why we see the progress we do."
## Compressed Summary
- AI adoption is progressing from chatbots and reasoners to autonomous organizations.
- Prompt engineering and cached inputs create bottlenecks and high costs in agent workflows.
- Enterprises should treat AI models like codebases with test cases, evals, and traces.
- Custom knowledge work models allow companies to bake implicit institutional knowledge into model weights.
- Nightly loops enable automated continuous learning and checkpoint improvement.
- **Keywords**: agents, evals, training, routing, continual-learning
- **Core insight**: Organizations must transition from relying on prompt engineering and cached context to training custom models on their own data and workflows, establishing continuous feedback loops to compound institutional knowledge into model weights.
